Abstract

The remarkable success of score-based diffusion models has spurred significant efforts to establish their theoretical foundations. However, existing complexity bounds for score approximation rely heavily on restrictive assumptions like Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports, which are routinely violated by the singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters inherent to real-world perceptual data. This work establishes a universal score approximation theorem that works for any distribution supported on any compact set of upper Minkowski dimension dd. Using a novel discrete-mixture formulation, we prove that the score function can be approximated with a ReLU network whose complexity grows exponentially only with dd, thus breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality. Combined with existing theories on accurately solving the backward diffusion SDE for arbitrary compact distributions, our work shows that diffusion models readily adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures, explaining their competence in real-world generative tasks.

1 Introduction

In machine learning, researchers are always enthusiastic about unraveling the theory behind a novel model or structure that achieves groundbreaking empirical success. We have seen this trend with Resnet Lin and Jegelka [2018] and transformers Geshkovski et al. [2025] Bergsträßer et al. [2025], and the field of score-based diffusion models is no exception: ever since its introduction Ho et al. [2020] Song and Ermon [2019] Song et al. [2021] around 2020, solid research has established error bounds for using diffusion models to reconstruct a smooth distribution Zhang et al. [2024] Oko et al. [2023], discretizing the backward diffusion process using numerical SDE solvers Bortoli [2022] Lee et al. [2022] Lee et al. [2023], and using ReLU networks to approximate the score function Chen et al. [2023a] Zhang et al. [2026].

A very common assumption for theoretical papers on machine learning to make is that the target function they seek to approximate exhibits some degree of smoothness or continuity, and the field of score-based diffusion models is also no exception: Chen et al. [2023b], Lee et al. [2022], Chen et al. [2023a] all assume the underlying distribution p0p_{0} to have Lipschitz score or Lipschitz on-support score (in case where p0p_{0} is supported on a linear subspace in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}), while Oko et al. [2023], Zhang et al. [2024], Zhang et al. [2026], respectively, require p0p_{0} to be smooth in the Besov, Sobolev, or Holder sense; Conforti et al. [2025] Bruno and Sabanis [2025] attempt to slightly relax the smoothness condition, but still require p0p_{0} to be differentiable almost everywhere. To the best of our knowledge, Bortoli [2022] and Lee et al. [2023], which provide convergence results for numerically solving the backward diffusion SDE, are the only works that consider arbitrary distributions with compact support. However, this commonly held assumption can prove slightly disappointing–both in practice and in theory–for the reasons below.

Practically, real-world image distributions are characterized by singularities von Rohrscheidt and Rieck [2022] Lim et al. [2025] and sharp boundaries Belkin et al. [2012] near which the density function abruptly changes. Indeed, the simple fact that RGB pixel intensities are bounded and often clip abruptly at 0 or 255 alone creates step-like discontinuities, breaking standard continuity assumptions. Theoretically, mitigating the problems posed by discontinuous densities and spiky gradients in the data distribution was one of the reasons why diffusion models introduce Gaussian noise–and with many different magnitudes–in the first place Song and Ermon [2019]. While small noise scales would still result in score blowup around discontinuities Song and Ermon [2019] Chen et al. [2023a], such problems were taken into consideration when works on diffusion models introduce early stopping Lee et al. [2022], set error tolerance

Ept​‖∇log⁡pt​(x)−∇log⁡pt,a​p​p​r​(x)‖22\displaystyle\mathrm{E}_{p_{t}}\left\|\nabla\log p_{t}(x)-\nabla\log p_{t,appr}(x)\right\|_{2}^{2} (1)

to ϵ2/σ4​(t){\epsilon^{2}}/{\sigma^{4}(t)} or ϵ2/σ2​(t){\epsilon^{2}}/{\sigma^{2}(t)} (rather than a fixed constant ϵ2\epsilon^{2}) at time tt Chen et al. [2023a] Zhang et al. [2026], and require convergence in W2W_{2} rather than TV\mathrm{TV} distance when handling distributions supported on manifolds Lee et al. [2023] Chen et al. [2023a]. Demanding the underlying distribution to already be sufficiently smooth, even after the above relaxations of requirements, is akin to proving a master chef can prepare a banquet assuming all meat and vegetables arrive trimmed, sliced, sauced, and seasoned: while technically correct, it ignores the fundamental purpose of hiring a chef.

In contrast, this work establishes the first theory for score approximation that considers any distribution in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} supported on a compact set of upper Minkowski dimension dd (i.e. supp⁡(p0)\mathrm{supp}(p_{0}) can be covered by CK​r−dC_{K}r^{-d} balls of radius rr for all rr small enough). The main contributions of our theory include:

  • •

    We present the first score approximation theory that works on any distribution with compact support, significantly widening the scope of existing score approximation theories by removing all continuity and smoothness assumptions.

  • •

    The parameter size of our neural network grows with ϵ\epsilon at order roughly 𝒪(ϵ−d/2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-d/2}). This successfully removes exponential dependence on ambient dimensionality, and is more ideal than what existing works derive when assuming p0p_{0} to have Lipschitz on-support score Chen et al. [2023a], or p0p_{0} to be lower bounded and β\beta-Holder continuous with β<2\beta<2 Zhang et al. [2026].

  • •

    Our divide-and-conquer tactic to bound the discretization error in Theorem 2, as well as our results on C1,C2,rC_{1},C_{2},r-regularity in Theorem 3, can be adapted to bound the higher order derivatives of log⁡pt​(x)\log p_{t}(x) on a set of arbitrarily large measure (See Section 5 for a detailed discussion). This can be helpful for many works on diffusion theory Lee et al. [2022] Lee et al. [2023].

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 Score Based Diffusion Models

Since the introduction of Score-based Generative Modeling Song and Ermon [2019] and DDPM Ho et al. [2020], pioneering works of Song, Sohl-Dickstein, and Kingma Song et al. [2021], Song, Dhariwal, and Chen Song et al. [2023], Dhariwal and Nichol Dhariwal and Nichol [2021], and many others have established an empirically verified framework for overcoming the challenges posed by sharp gradients, high-curvature manifold supports, and fragmented typical sets Song and Ermon [2019] common in high-dimensional generative tasks: using a forward process to gradually smooth the data distribution by injecting different layers of Gaussian noise, and using a backward process to iteratively remove noise from the corrupted sample using a trained denoising network.

More specifically, given a set of data points satisfying an unknown distribution p0p_{0} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, the forward process corrupts p0p_{0} with Gaussian noise by having sample points undergo the forward Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE)

d​x=−α⁡(t)​x​d​t+β⁡(t)​d​w,t∈[0,T]\displaystyle dx=-\alpha(t)xdt+\beta(t)dw,t\in[0,T] (2)

with ww the nn-dimensional standard Brownian motion, and TT large enough such that the marginal distribution pTp_{T} at time TT effectively becomes a known Gaussian distribution. Under such perturbation, a random sample point x⁡(t)x(t) at time tt can be expressed as the sum

x⁡(t)=k−1​(t)​xs​i​g+σ⁡(t)​xn​o​i​s​e,x(t)=k^{-1}(t)x_{sig}+\sigma(t)x_{noise},

where

xs​i​g∼p0,xn​o​i​s​e∼𝒩⁡(0,In),k⁡(t)=e∫0tα⁡(s)​𝑑s,σ2​(0)=0,and​d​σ2d​t=β2​(t)−2​α​(t)​σ2​(t)x_{sig}\sim p_{0},x_{noise}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}),k(t)=e^{\int_{0}^{t}\alpha(s)ds},\sigma^{2}(0)=0,\mathrm{and}\ \frac{d\sigma^{2}}{dt}=\beta^{2}(t)-2\alpha(t)\sigma^{2}(t)

with initial condition σ2​(0)=0\sigma^{2}(0)=0. As a result, defining the scaling operator (τk∘f)​(x)=kn​f​(k​x)(\tau_{k}\circ f)(x)=k^{n}f(kx), the marginal distribution ptp_{t} admits the expression

pt=(τk⁡(t)∘p0)∗φσ2​(t),p_{t}=(\tau_{k(t)}\circ p_{0})*\varphi_{\sigma^{2}(t)},

showing that all positive choices for α\alpha and β\beta create distributions equivalent up to a space-based rescaling and time-based reparameterization Lee et al. [2022] Zhang et al. [2024]. As such, we assume the VE perturbation scheme (α⁡(t)=0,β⁡(t)=1\alpha(t)=0,\beta(t)=1) unless otherwise specified.

The backward process, meanwhile, iteratively removes noise from corrupted samples by solving the backward diffusion SDE

dx~=−[α(t)x+β2(t)∇logpt(x)]dt+β(t)dw^;x~(T)∼𝒩(0,σ2(T)In)≈pTd\tilde{x}=-[\alpha(t)x+\beta^{2}(t)\nabla\log p_{t}(x)]dt+\beta(t)d\hat{w};\ \ \tilde{x}(T)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}(T)I_{n})\approx p_{T}

[2023].

2.2 Prior Theoretical Guarantees

Current theoretical analysis for score-based diffusion models mainly follow on one of the three topics below:

  1. 1.

    Given sufficient resource, how well can a score-based diffusion model reconstruct the underlying distribution using a finite number of data points?

  2. 2.

    Given an accurate enough score estimator, how many numerical steps do score-based diffusion models need in order to converge to the underlying distribution?

  3. 3.

    Given constraints on network size and depth, how well can a neural network approximate the score function ∇log⁡pt​(x)\nabla\log p_{t}(x)?

Question 1 has been studied by Oko et al. [2023], Chen et al. [2023a] and is the main focus of Zhang et al. [2024], which proves that score-based diffusion models are minimax optimal at reconstructing distributions inside the β\beta-Sobolev (β≤2\beta\leq 2) space and with sub-Gaussian tails. Question 2 has been studied by Lee et al. [2022], Chen et al. [2023a], Bortoli [2022], and critically, Lee et al. [2023], which proves that for any underlying distribution p0p_{0} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with compact support of diameter RR, exponential integrators for the backward process can converge in 𝒪⁡(Poly⁡(d,R,1/ϵ))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{Poly}(d,R,1/\epsilon)) steps to a distribution qq such that T​V​(q,p~)<ϵ,W2​(p~,p0)<ϵTV(q,\tilde{p})<\epsilon,W_{2}(\tilde{p},p_{0})<\epsilon for some intermediate distribution p~\tilde{p}. That is, we can accurately reconstruct any compact distribution in a polynomial number of steps simply by accurately approximating its score function ∇log⁡pt​(x)\nabla\log p_{t}(x).

In comparison, question 3 has received notably less attention and yielded limited results. Traditional results for approximating general functions on compact sets Opschoor et al. [2021] also apply to the score function. However, their bounds on the network size almost always grow exponentially with the ambient dimensionality, becoming inefficient and impractical for high-dimensional image distributions satisfying the manifold hypothesis. Chen et al. [2023a] presents a score matching network with size independent of the ambient dimensionality, but their assumption–that the data distribution is concentrated on a dd-dimensional linear space of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}–is a significant simplification of the manifold hypothesis seldom satisfied for real-world videos or images.

To the best of our knowledge, the most meaningful advancement in this direction is a concurrent work Zhang et al. [2026], which expands the results of Chen et al. [2023a] to CβC^{\beta} smooth, lower and upper bounded distributions concentrated on compact d−d-dimensional manifolds with positive reach, embedded in the sample space ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Using geometric techniques, Zhang et al. [2026] proves that such distributions can be approximated with mean square error 𝒪⁡(n2​γ+d+2​δ2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2\gamma+d+2}\delta^{2}) using a neural network of size 𝒪⁡(1/δd/β)\mathcal{O}(1/\delta^{{d}/{\beta}}), which translates to a network size of 𝒪⁡(nd2/2​β​n(γ+1)​d/β​(1/ϵ)d/β)\mathcal{O}(n^{{d^{2}}/{2\beta}}n^{(\gamma+1)d/\beta}(1/\epsilon)^{{d}/{\beta}}) to achieve error tolerance ϵ\epsilon. Aside from the fact that nd2/2​βn^{{d^{2}}/{2\beta}} may grow super-exponentially for moderately smooth (β≤2\beta\leq 2) distributions, Zhang et al. [2026] presents an impressive result for approximating the score function of highly smooth data distributions concentrated on smooth, low-dimensional manifolds.

Our work further advances the state-of-the-art by trading differential geometry for an analytics-heavy approach that focuses on the smoothing effect and asymptotic behavior of Gaussian kernels. Using a distinct decomposition that simplifies ptp_{t} into a Gaussian mixture, our work proves that any distribution with compact support of upper Minkowski dimension dd can be approximated with L2L^{2} error ϵ\epsilon using a network of size 𝒪⁡(n3​d/4​(1/ϵ)d/2)\mathcal{O}(n^{{3d}/{4}}(1/\epsilon)^{{d}/{2}}). Compared to Zhang et al. [2026], we relaxed the super-exponential nd2/2​βn^{d^{2}/2\beta} to a more manageable n3​d/4n^{3d/4}, and further expanded the applicable family of distributions, taking the current theory of score approximation one step closer to real-world applicability.

3 Main Results and Theorem Statements

We establish our central result by demonstrating that the score function can be accurately and efficiently approximated for any compactly supported distribution, avoiding the exponential dependence on the ambient dimension nn.

Theorem 1 (Universal Score Approximation).

Let p0p_{0} be a probability distribution in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} such that supp⁡(p0)\mathrm{supp}({p_{0}}) is compact with diameter RR and upper Minkowski dimension dd (i.e., for all r<1r<1, supp⁡(p0)\mathrm{supp}({p_{0}}) can be covered by no more than CK​r−dC_{K}r^{-d} balls of radius rr). Under the Variance Exploding (VE) perturbation scheme (k⁡(t)=1;σ2​(t)=tk(t)=1;\sigma^{2}(t)=t), for any target error ϵ<min⁡{1,R/5​t0}\epsilon<\min\{1,R/5t_{0}\} and early stopping time t0<1t_{0}<1, the true score function ∇log⁡pt​(x)\nabla\log p_{t}(x) can be approximated via the data-prediction formulation

∇log⁡pt,a​p​p​r​(x)=sθ​(x,t)−xt\displaystyle\nabla\log p_{t,appr}(x)=\frac{s_{\theta}(x,t)-x}{t}

such that the mean squared error satisfies

Ept​(x)​‖∇log⁡pt​(x)−∇log⁡pt,a​p​p​r​(x)‖22≤7​ϵ2,∀t∈[t0,T].\displaystyle\mathrm{E}_{p_{t}(x)}\left\|\nabla\log p_{t}(x)-\nabla\log p_{t,appr}(x)\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq 7\epsilon^{2},\quad\forall t\in[t_{0},T].

This approximation is achieved using a fully connected ReLU network sθ​(x,t)s_{\theta}(x,t) of depth 𝒪⁡(log⁡ω⁡(ϵ)​log⁡log⁡ω⁡(ϵ))\mathcal{O}\big(\log\omega(\epsilon)\log\log\omega(\epsilon)\big) and width 𝒪⁡(CK​r−d​(n​log⁡ω⁡(ϵ)+log2⁡ω⁡(ϵ)))\mathcal{O}\big(C_{K}r^{-d}\left(n\log\omega(\epsilon)+\log^{2}\omega(\epsilon)\right)\big), where

r=t03/4​ϵ1/260​λ​(ϵ)3/2,ω⁡(ϵ)=n​CK​(R+λ⁡(ϵ)​T)rd​t0​ϵ,\displaystyle r=\frac{t_{0}^{3/4}\epsilon^{1/2}}{60\lambda(\epsilon)^{3/2}},\quad\omega(\epsilon)=\frac{nC_{K}(R+\lambda(\epsilon)\sqrt{T})}{r^{d}t_{0}\epsilon},

with the concentration parameter λ⁡(ϵ)\lambda(\epsilon) defined as 11 1 Expression of λ⁡(ϵ)\lambda(\epsilon) differs from that in 2, as λ⁡(ϵ)\lambda(\epsilon) must also ensure that P⁡(‖x⁡(t)−x⁡(0)‖>λ⁡(ϵ)​t)P(\left\|x(t)-x(0)\right\|>\lambda(\epsilon)\sqrt{t}) is smaller than (ϵ​t0/R)2(\epsilon t_{0}/R)^{2} via the Gaussian Concentration Inequality. λ⁡(ϵ)=94​n+8​log⁡Rϵ+13​log⁡CK+max⁡{d,14}+22​log⁡1t0+2.\displaystyle\lambda(\epsilon)=\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}n+8\log\frac{R}{\epsilon}+\frac{1}{3}\log{C_{K}}+\frac{\max\{d,14\}+2}{2}\log\frac{1}{t_{0}}}+2.

For practical configurations involving high-dimensional data, the ambient dimension nn strictly dominates dd, and the terms log⁡(R/ϵ),log⁡CK,\log(R/\epsilon),\log C_{K}, and log⁡(1/t0)\log(1/t_{0}) contribute only logarithmically. In such regimes, λ⁡(ϵ)\lambda(\epsilon) scales proportionally to n\sqrt{n}, bounding the parameter size of sθ​(x,t)s_{\theta}(x,t) at the order of 𝒪⁡(n​d​(n3/4ϵ1/2​t03/4)d)\mathcal{O}\big(nd(\frac{n^{3/4}}{\epsilon^{1/2}t_{0}^{3/4}})^{d}\big). This confirms that the network complexity depends strictly polynomially on the ambient dimension nn, absorbing the exponential blowup entirely into the intrinsic dimension dd.

Theorem 1 is proven by rigorously analyzing the discretization of the exact score function into a finite Gaussian mixture (CC abbreviates the Gaussian factor 2​π​t−n2\sqrt{2\pi t}^{-\frac{n}{2}}):

∇log⁡pt​(x)=∑i=1K⁡(r)wi​∫ℝnC​e−‖x−y‖22​t​y−xt​d​pi​(y)∑i=1K⁡(r)wi​∫ℝnC​e−‖x−y‖22​t​d​pi​(y)≈∑i=1K⁡(r)wi​C​e−‖x−y~i‖22​t​y~i−xt∑i=1K⁡(r)wi​C​e−‖x−y~i‖22​t\displaystyle\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K(r)}w_{i}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}Ce^{-\frac{\left\|x-y\right\|^{2}}{2t}}\frac{y-x}{t}dp_{i}(y)}{\sum_{i=1}^{K(r)}w_{i}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}Ce^{-\frac{\left\|x-y\right\|^{2}}{2t}}dp_{i}(y)}\approx\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K(r)}w_{i}Ce^{-\frac{\left\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\right\|^{2}}{2t}}\frac{\tilde{y}_{i}-x}{t}}{\sum_{i=1}^{K(r)}w_{i}Ce^{-\frac{\left\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\right\|^{2}}{2t}}} (3)

where we decompose p0=∑i=1K⁡(r)wi​pip_{0}=\sum_{i=1}^{K(r)}w_{i}p_{i} such that 22 2 Starting from formula 3, all balls B⁡(x,r)B(x,r) are considered closed balls and all norms ‖x‖\left\|x\right\| are considered 2-norms, unless otherwise specified supp⁡(pi)⊆B⁡(yi,r)\mathrm{supp}(p_{i})\subseteq B(y_{i},r) and denote the local means as y~i=Epi​[y]\tilde{y}_{i}=\mathrm{E}_{p_{i}}[y]. Note that such a spatial decomposition trivially exists for any covering, as unlike in general partition of unity theorems, we do not impose any smoothness assumptions on the sub-distributions {pi}\{p_{i}\}.

To formalize the accuracy of formula 3, we introduce a weak regularity condition that prevents the probability mass from collapsing in an unmeasurable manner.

Definition 1.

Given a measure μ\mu on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, a point xx is called C1,C2,rC_{1},C_{2},r-regular under μ\mu if there exists a center x0x_{0} such that x∈B⁡(x0,r)x\in B(x_{0},r), and

C1⋅eC2​‖x0−y‖2r​μ​(B⁡(x0,r))>μ⁡(B⁡(y,r)),∀y∈ℝn.\displaystyle C_{1}\cdot e^{C_{2}\frac{\left\|x_{0}-y\right\|_{2}}{r}}\mu(B(x_{0},r))>\mu(B(y,r)),\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. (4)

While lower and upper bounded distributions, as well as distributions with Hölder-continuous log density, naturally satisfy this condition, it is equally satisfied by highly irregular, fractal-like distributions which do not even admit a probability density function.

Example 1.

Consider the Cantor measure μ\mu on [0,1][0,1], uniquely determined by the recursive interval removal, mapping to the formula:

Thus, for any r∈[13n,13n−1]r\in[\frac{1}{3^{n}},\frac{1}{3^{n-1}}], we have 12n≤μ⁡(B⁡(x0,r))≤12n−1\frac{1}{2^{n}}\leq\mu(B(x_{0},r))\leq\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}. This strictly bounds the mass ratio, yielding 2​μ​(B⁡(x0,r))≥μ⁡(B⁡(y0,r))2\mu(B(x_{0},r))\geq\mu(B(y_{0},r)) for all x0,y0∈supp⁡(μ)x_{0},y_{0}\in\mathrm{supp}(\mu). Consequently, for any arbitrary radius rr, x∼μx\sim\mu is 2,0,r2,0,r-regular with probability 1.

Given the above definition of regularity, the proof of Theorem 1 is structurally divided into three sub-theorems. First, we show that the discretization error is tightly bounded as long as the corrupted point xx remains reasonably close to a regular point.

Theorem 2 (Discretization Error).

Let p0p_{0} be defined as in Theorem 1. Under the VE perturbation scheme, by choosing

λ⁡(ϵ)≥52​C2+13​log⁡C1​CKϵ+(d2+1)​log⁡1t0+2;r=t034​ϵ1260​λ​(ϵ)32;\lambda(\epsilon)\geq\sqrt{\frac{5}{2}C_{2}+\frac{1}{3}\log\frac{C_{1}C_{K}}{\epsilon}+(\frac{d}{2}+1)\log\frac{1}{t_{0}}}+2;r=\frac{t_{0}^{\frac{3}{4}}\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}}{60\lambda(\epsilon)^{\frac{3}{2}}};

the discrete approximation in Equation 3 satisfies the following:

  • •

    For any C1,C2,λ⁡(ϵ)​tC_{1},C_{2},\lambda(\epsilon)\sqrt{t}-regular point x0x_{0}, and for all x∈B⁡(x0,λ⁡(ϵ)​t−2​r)x\in B(x_{0},\lambda(\epsilon)\sqrt{t}-2r), ∇log⁡pt​(x)\nabla\log p_{t}(x) is approximated with error bounded by ϵ\epsilon.

  • •

    For all x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the approximation error is globally bounded by Rt\frac{R}{t}.

To ensure the local error bound from Theorem 2 holds almost everywhere, we prove that our regularity condition is not a restrictive assumption, but rather a universal property of compact distributions.

Theorem 3 (Universal Regularity).

Let μ\mu be an arbitrary probability distribution in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with compact support. For any fixed radius rr, define UδU_{\delta} to be the set of points that are e3​n​1δ,n2,re^{3n}\frac{1}{\delta},\frac{n}{2},r-regular under μ\mu, then μ⁡(Uδ)>1−δ.\mu(U_{\delta})>1-\delta.

By choosing δ\delta sufficiently small and λ⁡(ϵ)>n+2​2​log⁡(R/ϵ​t0)\lambda(\epsilon)>\sqrt{n}+2\sqrt{2\log(R/\epsilon t_{0})}, Theorem 3, along with the Gaussian Concentration Inequality, ensures that a noisy sample x∼ptx\sim p_{t} lands inside the high-accuracy basin of a regular point with overwhelming probability. Finally, we demonstrate that the discrete mixture can be precisely implemented by a neural network.

Theorem 4 (Network Approximation).

Define VJ=supp⁡(p0)+B⁡(0,J).V_{J}=\mathrm{supp}(p_{0})+B(0,J). The discrete expectation

∑i=1K⁡(r)wi​e−‖x−y~i‖222​t​(y~i)∑i=1K⁡(r)wi​e−‖x−y~i‖222​t\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K(r)}w_{i}e^{-\frac{\left\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}({\tilde{y}_{i}})}{\sum_{i=1}^{K(r)}w_{i}e^{-\frac{\left\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}} (5)

can be approximated with error ≤t0​ϵ\leq t_{0}\epsilon for all (t,x)∈[t0,T]×VJ(t,x)\in[t_{0},T]\times V_{J}, using a ReLU network whose output remain strictly within Conv⁡(supp⁡(p0))+B⁡(0,t0​ϵ)\mathrm{Conv(\mathrm{supp}(p_{0}))}+B(0,t_{0}\epsilon) across the entire ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. The depth and width of the network are bounded by 𝒪⁡(log⁡ω​log⁡log​ω)\mathcal{O}\big(\log\omega\log\log\omega\big) and 𝒪⁡(K⁡(r)​(n​log⁡ω+log2⁡ω))\mathcal{O}\big(K(r)(n\log\omega+\log^{2}\omega)\big), respectively, where we define

ω=n​K​(r)​(R+J)t0​ϵ.\omega=\frac{nK(r)(R+J)}{t_{0}\epsilon}.

4 Proof Overview

In this section, we outline the mathematical intuition behind theorems 2, 3, 4. Full constructive proofs for theorems 2, 3, and 4, as well as the relatively straightforward proof of theorem 1 from the three sub-theorems, are deferred to the Appendix.

4.1 Proof Sketch of Theorem 2

Let p0=∑i=1Kwi​pip_{0}=\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}p_{i} be the decomposition with supp⁡(pi)⊆B⁡(yi,r)\operatorname{supp}(p_{i})\subseteq B(y_{i},r), and set y~i=𝔼pi​[y]\tilde{y}_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{i}}[y]. For a fixed xx, write the true score and the approximation as

∇log⁡pt​(x)=∑iwipi,t(x)∇logpi,t(x)∑iwi​pi,t​(x),∇log⁡pt,appr​(x)=∑iwi​e−‖x−y~i‖22​t​y~i−xt∑iwi​e−‖x−y~i‖22​t,\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}p_{i,t}(x)\nabla\log p_{i,t}(x)}{\sum_{i}w_{i}p_{i,t}(x)},\qquad\nabla\log p_{t,\mathrm{appr}}(x)=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}e^{-\frac{\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\|^{2}}{2t}}\frac{\tilde{y}_{i}-x}{t}}{\sum_{i}w_{i}e^{-\frac{\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\|^{2}}{2t}}},

where pi,t​(x)=∫pi​(y)​e−‖y−x‖22​t​𝑑yp_{i,t}(x)=\int p_{i}(y)e^{-\frac{\|y-x\|^{2}}{2t}}dy and ∇log⁡pi,t​(x)\nabla\log p_{i,t}(x) is defined analogously.

Single‑kernel error.

Taylor‑expand the Gaussian kernel around y~i\tilde{y}_{i} inside each integral:

e−‖y−x‖22​t=e−‖y~i−x‖22​t​[1+⟨y−y~i,x−y~it⟩+12​(y−y~i)⊤​∇y2e−‖y′−x‖22​t​(y−y~i)].e^{-\frac{\|y-x\|^{2}}{2t}}=e^{-\frac{\|\tilde{y}_{i}-x\|^{2}}{2t}}\Bigl[1+\bigl\langle y-\tilde{y}_{i},\frac{x-\tilde{y}_{i}}{t}\bigr\rangle+\frac{1}{2}(y-\tilde{y}_{i})^{\top}\nabla_{y}^{2}e^{-\frac{\|y^{\prime}-x\|^{2}}{2t}}(y-\tilde{y}_{i})\Bigr].

As 𝔼pi​[y]=y~i\mathbb{E}_{p_{i}}[y]=\tilde{y}_{i}, the first‑order term integrates to 0. As supp⁡(pi)⊆B⁡(y~i,2​r)\operatorname{supp}(p_{i})\subseteq B(\tilde{y}_{i},2r), the remainder gives

|pi,t​(x)−e−‖x−y~i‖22​t|≤2​r2​e−(‖x−yi‖−r)22​t​(‖x−yi‖+r)2+tt2.\bigl|p_{i,t}(x)-e^{-\frac{\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\|^{2}}{2t}}\bigr|\leq 2r^{2}\,e^{-\frac{(\|x-y_{i}\|-r)^{2}}{2t}}\frac{(\|x-y_{i}\|+r)^{2}+t}{t^{2}}.

A similar computation for the numerator yields

‖∇log⁡pi,t​(x)−y~i−xt‖≤min⁡{e(‖x−yi‖+r)2−(‖x−yi‖−r)22​t​‖x−yi‖+rt2​(4​r2),2​rt}.\bigl\|\nabla\log p_{i,t}(x)-\tfrac{\tilde{y}_{i}-x}{t}\bigr\|\leq\min\!\Bigl\{e^{\frac{(\|x-y_{i}\|+r)^{2}-(\|x-y_{i}\|-r)^{2}}{2t}}\frac{\|x-y_{i}\|+r}{t^{2}}(4r^{2}),\;\frac{2r}{t}\Bigr\}.

These bounds are small when ‖x−yi‖/t\|x-y_{i}\|/\sqrt{t} is moderate, but can blow up when xx is far from the kernel center.

Decomposition into near and far groups.

Fix a large λ⁡(ϵ)\lambda(\epsilon) and small rr (to be chosen later). Consider an xx within distance λ​t−2​r\lambda\sqrt{t}-2r of a (C1,C2,λ​t)(C_{1},C_{2},\lambda\sqrt{t})-regular point. By definition of regularity, there exists a ball B⁡(x0,λ​t)B(x_{0},\lambda\sqrt{t}) satisfying 4 such that ‖x−x0‖≤2​λ​t−2​r\|x-x_{0}\|\leq 2\lambda\sqrt{t}-2r.

We cluster the balls {B⁡(xi,r)}i=1K\{B(x_{i},r)\}_{i=1}^{K} into near group and far group as follows. First, single out the near-group balls close to xx

A0={i|xi∈B⁡(x,5​λ​t−2​r)},A~0={i|xi∈B⁡(x,3​λ​t−r)}.A_{0}=\{i|x_{i}\in B(x,5\lambda\sqrt{t}-2r)\},\tilde{A}_{0}=\{i|x_{i}\in B(x,3\lambda\sqrt{t}-r)\}.

Then, cover the far-region supp⁡(p0)\B⁡(x,5​λ​t−2​r)\mathrm{supp}(p_{0})\backslash B(x,5\lambda\sqrt{t}-2r) with balls {Bj}j=1N\{B_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} of radius λ​t−r\lambda\sqrt{t}-r, N≤CK​(λ​t−r)−dN\leq C_{K}(\lambda\sqrt{t}-r)^{-d}. Using a geometric pushing argument detailed in the appendix, we can assume their centers zjz_{j} satisfy ‖zj−x‖>24​(λ​t−r)\|z_{j}-x\|>\sqrt{24}(\lambda\sqrt{t}-r).

Finally, partition {1,…,K}\A0\{1,...,K\}\backslash A_{0} into sets A1,…,ANA_{1},...,A_{N} such that xi∈Bjx_{i}\in B_{j} holds for all i∈Aji\in A_{j}. We shall now be able to control the total mass contribution of all balls inside a far group AjA_{j}.

Bounding far groups.

For a far group AjA_{j}, the relative error of replacing the exact integrals by point‑mass evaluations is large, but the Gaussian weight is tiny. Using the regularity condition and the fact that ‖x−y~i‖≤3​λ​t\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\|\leq 3\lambda\sqrt{t} for i∈A~0i\in\tilde{A}_{0} while ‖x−y~i‖≥‖zj−x‖−λ​t\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\|\geq\|z_{j}-x\|-\lambda\sqrt{t} for i∈Aji\in A_{j}, we obtain

C1​eC2​‖zj−x‖+2​λ​tλ​t​∑i∈A~0wi​e−‖x−y~i‖22​t≥e(‖zj−x‖−λ​t)2−(3​λ​t)22​t​∑i∈Ajwi​e−‖x−y~i‖22​t.C_{1}e^{C_{2}\frac{\|z_{j}-x\|+2\lambda\sqrt{t}}{\lambda\sqrt{t}}}\sum_{i\in\tilde{A}_{0}}w_{i}e^{-\frac{\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\|^{2}}{2t}}\;\geq\;e^{\frac{(\|z_{j}-x\|-\lambda\sqrt{t})^{2}-(3\lambda\sqrt{t})^{2}}{2t}}\sum_{i\in A_{j}}w_{i}e^{-\frac{\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\|^{2}}{2t}}.

Since A~0⊆A0\tilde{A}_{0}\subseteq A_{0}, this inequality bounds the far‑group denominator in terms of the near‑group denominator multiplied by an exponential factor. After combining with the per‑kernel error bounds and summing over all far groups AjA_{j}, the total contribution from far groups to both the mass difference and the gradient term is bounded by ∑i∈A0wi​e−‖x−y~i‖22​t\sum_{i\in A_{0}}w_{i}e^{-\frac{\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\|^{2}}{2t}} times quantities D⁡(λ)D(\lambda) and D~​(λ)\tilde{D}(\lambda) that, for λ>max⁡{1,C2}\lambda>\max\{1,\sqrt{C_{2}}\} and r<t/2r<\sqrt{t}/2, decay super‑exponentially in λ\lambda:

D(λ)∼C1r2λ2t−1e7​C2−3​λ2,D~(λ)∼C1e7​C2−3​λ2rt+C1r2λ3t−3/2e7​C2−3​λ2.D(\lambda)\sim C_{1}r^{2}\lambda^{2}t^{-1}e^{7C_{2}-3\lambda^{2}},\qquad\tilde{D}(\lambda)\sim C_{1}e^{7C_{2}-3\lambda^{2}}\tfrac{r}{t}+C_{1}r^{2}\lambda^{3}t^{-3/2}e^{7C_{2}-3\lambda^{2}}.

Assembling the multi‑kernel error.

The total approximation error is bounded by the sum of two terms (one from numerator, one from denominator). After splitting the sums into near and far groups and using the above estimates, the near‑group part contributes an error of order

e10​λ​rt​(20​r2​λ​tt2+50​r2​λ2+2​r2t⋅5​λ​tt),e^{\frac{10\lambda r}{\sqrt{t}}}\Bigl(\frac{20r^{2}\lambda\sqrt{t}}{t^{2}}+\frac{50r^{2}\lambda^{2}+2r^{2}}{t}\cdot\frac{5\lambda\sqrt{t}}{t}\Bigr),

while the far‑group part adds terms involving D​(λ),D~​(λ)D(\lambda),\tilde{D}(\lambda) multiplied by the covering number (λ​t−r)−d(\lambda\sqrt{t}-r)^{-d} and an additional factor of λ/t\lambda/\sqrt{t}. The second term (ratio of mass differences times the score norm) is handled similarly, with the denominator relative error controlled by a geometric series.

Choosing λ\lambda and rr.

To make the overall error less than ϵ\epsilon for all t∈[t0,T]t\in[t_{0},T], it suffices to enforce six inequalities, including e10​λ​r/t<1.2e^{10\lambda r/\sqrt{t}}<1.2, bounds on the near‑field polynomial, and bounds on far‑field exponential terms. These are simultaneously satisfied for all t∈[t0,T]t\in[t_{0},T] by taking our stated choices for λ\lambda and rr.

Out‑of‑distribution points.

For any xx farther than λ​t\lambda\sqrt{t} from the support (or not near a regular point), the trivial bound ‖∇log⁡pt​(x)‖≤R/t\|\nabla\log p_{t}(x)\|\leq R/t applies to both the true and approximate scores because t∇logpt(x)+xt\nabla\log p_{t}(x)+x and t∇logpt,appr(x)+xt\nabla\log p_{t,\mathrm{appr}}(x)+x both lie in the convex hull of the support, whose diameter is RR. Hence the global error never exceeds R/tR/t, which is already accounted for in the final L2L^{2} integration over the small‑probability region.

4.2 Proof Sketch of Theorem 3

We define a ball B⁡(x,r)B(x,r) as ”bad” if there exists a witness ball B⁡(y,r)B(y,r) such that

C1​eC2​‖x−y‖2r⋅μ⁡(B⁡(x,r))<μ⁡(B⁡(y,r))\displaystyle C_{1}e^{C_{2}\frac{\left\|x-y\right\|_{2}}{r}}\cdot\mu(B(x,r))<\mu(B(y,r)) (6)

Based on our definition, a point is C1,C2,rC_{1},C_{2},r-regular if there is any good ball containing it. Therefore, given a countable covering {B⁡(zi,r)}i=1∞\{B(z_{i},r)\}_{i=1}^{\infty} of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and denoting the set of all non-C1,C2,rC_{1},C_{2},r-regular points as VV, μ⁡(V)≤∑i∈Γμ⁡(B⁡(xi,r))\mu(V)\leq\sum_{i\in\Gamma}\mu(B(x_{i},r)), with Γ\Gamma the set of all indices corresponding to bad balls.

In the simple case where all ”bad” balls can be made to share the same witness B⁡(y0,r)B(y_{0},r), theorem 3 can be proven by setting the covering {B⁡(zi,r)}i=1∞\{B(z_{i},r)\}_{i=1}^{\infty} such that

{zi|i∈ℤ}={(2​j1​rn,…,2​jn​rn)|j1,…,jn∈ℤ}.\{z_{i}|i\in\mathbb{Z}\}=\{(\frac{2j_{1}r}{\sqrt{n}},...,\frac{2j_{n}r}{\sqrt{n}})|j_{1},...,j_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}\}.

In this case, 6 guarantees that the total measure of bad balls cannot exceed

∑j1,…,jn∈ℤ1C1​e−2​C2n​(j1−Y1)2+…+(jn−Yn)2,y0=(Y1,…,Yn)⋅2​rn;\sum_{j_{1},...,j_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}}\frac{1}{C_{1}}e^{-\frac{2C_{2}}{\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{(j_{1}-Y_{1})^{2}+...+(j_{n}-Y_{n})^{2}}},y_{0}=(Y_{1},...,Y_{n})\cdot\frac{2r}{\sqrt{n}};

a series convergent for all C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} due to the exponential decay term and can be upper bounded by 11 for C2=n/2C_{2}=n/2 and C1=e2​nC_{1}=e^{2n}. This result is easily generalizable to the case where ”bad” balls are mapped to witnesses that do not overlap.

We now reduce the general case to the non-overlapping witness case by iteratively re-allocating witnesses using a Vitali-style argument. Given a mapping gg from the center of bad balls UU to the center of their witnesses {yj}j∈𝒥\{y_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{J}}, we modify gg by greedily selecting a witness yky_{k} such that

μ⁡(B⁡(yk,r))≥(1−δ)​supj∈𝒥μ⁡(B⁡(yj,r)),\mu(B(y_{k},r))\geq(1-\delta)\sup_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\mu(B(y_{j},r)),

finding all points such that ‖g⁡(x)−yk‖2≤2​r\left\|g(x)-y_{k}\right\|_{2}\leq 2r, changing their image to yky_{k}, and then repeat the process. As supp⁡(μ)\mathrm{supp}(\mu) is compact, this process terminates after a finite iterations, and ensures that the image of each x∈Ux\in U is relocated at most once with maximal displacement 2​r2r. Thus, the resulting mapping GG is such that Im⁡(G)\mathrm{Im}(G) becomes a discrete set of points with pairwise distance >2​r>2r, and

C1​eC2​(‖x−y‖2r−2)⋅μ⁡(B⁡(x,r))<μ⁡(B⁡(G⁡(x),r)),C_{1}e^{C_{2}(\frac{\left\|x-y\right\|_{2}}{r}-2)}\cdot\mu(B(x,r))<\mu(B(G(x),r)),

allowing the proof to be finished by scaling up C1C_{1} to cancel out the e−2​C2e^{-2C_{2}} term.

4.3 Proof Sketch of Theorem 4

We rewrite the formula 5 as

⟨(y~1,…,y~K),Softmax⁡(log⁡w1−‖x−y~1‖222​t,…,log⁡wK−‖x−y~K‖222​t)⟩.\Big\langle(\tilde{y}_{1},...,\tilde{y}_{K}),\mathrm{Softmax}\Big(\log w_{1}-\frac{\left\|x-\tilde{y}_{1}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t},...,\log w_{K}-\frac{\left\|x-\tilde{y}_{K}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}\Big)\Big\rangle.

As {y~i}i=1K\{\tilde{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}; {log⁡wi}i=1K\{\log w_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} do not depend on xx, and can thus be baked into layer weights and biases, the greatest obstacle is that inputs of the Softmax function,

{zi}i=1K={log⁡w1−‖x−y~i‖222​t}i=1K,\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}=\Big\{\log w_{1}-\frac{\left\|x-\tilde{y}_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}\Big\}_{i=1}^{K},

can be hard to estimate, which we circumvent by designing a ReLU network that accurately approximates Softmax on the entire ℝK\mathbb{R}^{K}.

In fact, noting that

Softmax⁡(z1,…,zK)=Softmax⁡(z1−λ,z2−λ,…,zK−λ),\mathrm{Softmax}(z_{1},...,z_{K})=\mathrm{Softmax}(z_{1}-\lambda,z_{2}-\lambda,...,z_{K}-\lambda),

and that zm​a​x=max⁡{z1,…,zK}z_{max}=\max\{z_{1},...,z_{K}\} can be exactly approximated by recursively applying the formula

max⁡{z1,z2}=z1+ReLU⁡(z2−z1),\max\{z_{1},z_{2}\}=z_{1}+\mathrm{ReLU}(z_{2}-z_{1}),

we can deduct zm​a​xz_{max} from all input values, bounding the input domain to (−∞,0](-\infty,0]. In addition, this ensures that at least one input exactly equals 00, so the denominator ∑i=1Kezi−zm​a​x\sum_{i=1}^{K}e^{z_{i}-z_{max}} is lower bounded by 1. As a result, input values less that log⁡(δ​K2)\log(\delta K^{2}) can be completely ignored under error tolerance δ\delta.

Thus, the neural network approximation problem is, then, reduced to calculating:

  • •

    {‖x−yi‖22}i=1K\{\left\|x-y_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}\}_{i=1}^{K} (n​KnK calls of g⁡(x)=x2g(x)=x^{2}) on the interval [0,R+J][0,R+J].

  • •

    {ezi−zm​a​x}i=1K\{e^{z_{i}-z_{max}}\}_{i=1}^{K} (KK calls of h⁡(x)=exh(x)=e^{x}) on [−log⁡K2​δ,0][-\log K^{2}\delta,0],

  • •

    h⁡(t)=1/th(t)=1/t twice, once on [t0,T][t_{0},T] and once on [1,K][1,K]

each with some error tolerance δ\delta, results for which can be found in many established works on ReLU approximation capabilities Yarotsky [2017] Opschoor et al. [2021].

5 Conclusion

Can score-based diffusion models theoretically succeed on arbitrary compact data distributions, even in the absence of regularity assumptions? Their ubiquitous empirical success across diverse modalities–text, audio, image, video–strongly suggests they should; Bortoli [2022], Lee et al. [2023], prove that they can when given an accurate estimation of the score function. In this work, our rigorous theoretical framework finally proves that such an accurate estimation can always be provided.

It’s worth noting that our success in no way diminishes the accomplishments of prior theoretical guarantees based on continuity or smoothness assumptions. Instead, it provides a promising foundation for them to build upon. In fact, a direct calculation shows that the score ∇log⁡pt​(x)\nabla\log p_{t}(x), the Hessian ∇2​log​pt​(x)\nabla^{2}\log p_{t}(x), and other higher-order derivatives behave similarly to the discretization errors we analyzed. ∇2​log​pt​(x)\nabla^{2}\log p_{t}(x), for example, can be written as

∫ℝne−‖y−x‖222​t​(y−x)T​(y−x)−t​Int2​d​(p0​(y))∫ℝne−‖y−x‖222​t​d​(p0​(y))−(∫ℝne−‖y−x‖222​t​y−xt​d​(p0​(y))∫ℝne−‖y−x‖222​t​d​(p0​(y)))2,\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-\frac{\left\|y-x\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}\frac{(y-x)^{T}(y-x)-tI_{n}}{t^{2}}d(p_{0}(y))}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-\frac{\left\|y-x\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}d(p_{0}(y))}-\Big(\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-\frac{\left\|y-x\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}\frac{y-x}{t}d(p_{0}(y))}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-\frac{\left\|y-x\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}d(p_{0}(y))}\Big)^{2},

which can be effectively bounded simply by controlling the two terms

∫‖y−x‖>λ​te−‖y−x‖222​t​y−xt​d​(p0​(y))∫ℝne−‖y−x‖222​t​d​(p0​(y));∫‖y−x‖>λ​te−‖y−x‖222​t​(y−x)T​(y−x)−t​Int2​d​(p0​(y))∫ℝne−‖y−x‖222​t​d​(p0​(y)).\frac{\int_{\left\|y-x\right\|>\lambda\sqrt{t}}e^{-\frac{\left\|y-x\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}\frac{y-x}{t}d(p_{0}(y))}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-\frac{\left\|y-x\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}d(p_{0}(y))};\frac{\int_{\left\|y-x\right\|>\lambda\sqrt{t}}e^{-\frac{\left\|y-x\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}\frac{(y-x)^{T}(y-x)-tI_{n}}{t^{2}}d(p_{0}(y))}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-\frac{\left\|y-x\right\|_{2}^{2}}{2t}}d(p_{0}(y))}.

As a result, our divide-and-conquer tactic in Theorem 2, as well as our results regarding C1,C2,rC_{1},C_{2},r-regularity in Theorem 3, provide viable ways of actually bounding these terms after excluding a set of tiny probabilistic measure, rather than treating their boundedness only as an assumption. Meanwhile, strategies for handling ”bad sets” (using terminology from Lee et al. [2023]) of tiny measure have been extensively developed by prior theoretical works including Lee et al. [2023]. We believe that future research on diffusion models, building upon these techniques, will arrive at even more significant findings.
